findings.assertion: Three different measures appeared in the 20 August 1928 official publication. UNAM's historical transitory compilation labels the first decree (a multi-article judicial/congressional reform) effective 20 December 1928, while the THIRD decree, modifying Article 73(VI) to place Distrito Federal government under presidential authority, explicitly entered into force 1 January 1929. Applying the first decree's 20 December transitory to the municipal abolition would be a document-identity error.
findings.source_locator: IIJ-UNAM transitories, headings First Decree lines 3162–3167 vs Third Decree lines 3192–3201
findings.limitations: Historical transcription rather than original DOF; maintain distinction between enactment, promulgation and effective date; correct previous potential conflation.

findings.assertion: Obregón proposed ending Mexico City's elected municipal councils as early as 1921, but that attempt failed. Ziccardi traces renewed initiatives submitted on 18 April 1928, followed by a 12 May addition explicitly providing Congress's legislative authority and presidential government through statutory organs.
findings.source_locator: Ziccardi 2022 printed pp.75, 78, PDF text lines 997–1012 and 1031–1034
findings.limitations: Source is synthetic secondary analysis; original 1921 Senate file and April–May 1928 submissions not inspected.

findings.assertion: The 1928 confrontation was not simply modernizers versus defenders of inefficient government. Laborist deputy Vicente Lombardo Toledano argued that regional metropolitan services required coordination but opposed extinguishing political representation, discussing proportional or indirectly chosen representation tied to social organizations; other laborist deputies diverged over remedies.
findings.source_locator: Ziccardi 2022 printed pp.80–83, PDF text lines 1063–1101; Rico Ramírez thesis printed pp.77–79, lines 905–938
findings.limitations: Legislative speeches supplied through later scholars' transcriptions; not verified against original Diario de los Debates. Class/party motives remain interpretations.

findings.assertion: Two examined retrospective histories give INCOMPATIBLE tallies for the May 1928 vote over the proposed reform. Ziccardi reports first-round 170–22 and second-round 174–21 on 17 May; Rico Ramírez gives 185–21 for approval. Do not display a single unqualified vote count until the original May 17 legislative record resolves whether the texts summarize different motions or repeat an error.
findings.source_locator: Ziccardi 2022 printed p.84 text lines 1103–1106; Rico Ramírez thesis printed p.79 PDF text lines 929–935
findings.limitations: Explicit unresolved conflict: vote rounds, procedural stage, or transcription differ. This finding documents disagreement, not verified numeric result.

findings.assertion: Before the January 1929 statutory change took effect, the city's municipal government was already in crisis. Ziccardi reports obregonist resignations in the council in August 1928 and an interim municipal council with Carlos M. Esquerro and seven councillors, designated to serve until 31 December, replacing the old city cabildo's ordinary work.
findings.source_locator: Ziccardi 2022 printed pp.85–86, PDF text lines 1123–1144
findings.limitations: The source relies on 18 August 1928 Excélsior reporting, not yet inspected; distinguish proposal, legal appointment and actual working dates.

findings.assertion: The interim council's commissions included commerce, justice, finance, slaughterhouses/markets, public works, pulque/vehicles and entertainments; it studied sanitation works and reorganized policing. Ziccardi additionally reports suspension of work on the Palacio Municipal amid budget criticism. This offers a specific site-linked investigation at the Antiguo Palacio del Ayuntamiento, but not proof of which surviving architectural fabric was affected.
themes: Municipal services and unfinished Palacio Municipal works
findings.source_locator: Ziccardi 2022 printed pp.86–87, PDF text lines 1153–1163
findings.limitations: Contemporary municipal work orders/building plans and original newspaper issue unreviewed; no current room/architectural identification approved.

findings.assertion: A scholarly transcription of the 1928 Organic Law describes one Departamento Central built from former México, Tacuba, Tacubaya and Mixcoac municipality territories plus thirteen delegations including Ixtacalco, Ixtapalapa, General Anaya and others. Article 19 envisaged adjustments if continuous urban development blurred boundaries and public services became shared. This 1928 geography cannot be mapped using present-day alcaldía boundaries without a period map.
findings.source_locator: Rico Ramírez thesis print p.81, PDF text lines 952–966, checked scanned page image p85; Ziccardi 2022 printed p.88, lines 1173–1177
findings.limitations: Exact Article 19 original wording and inclusion of Ixtapalapa sections in central department vary by paraphrase; original law and contemporary cadastral map required.

findings.assertion: The proposed consultative-council structure offered participation chiefly through representatives of commercial, industrial, property and taxpayer organizations rather than elected municipal councillors. Rico Ramírez describes consultative oversight of works, services and taxes, while effective administrative authority remained with presidentially appointed officials.
findings.source_locator: Rico Ramírez thesis printed pp.79–82, text lines 940–969; selected p.81–82 page images checked
findings.limitations: Differentiate stated proposal, statutory institution, and actual composition in office; labor, tenant and Indigenous perspectives require separate evidence.

findings.assertion: Ziccardi records press praise for the temporary council in August–September 1928 but also later allegations of an unofficial treasury and municipal workers' concern over job loss. These illustrate contested administrative legitimacy rather than demonstrated reform success or proven misconduct.
themes: Urban administration, labor and press framing
findings.limitations: Journalistic charges and evaluations quoted by a secondary historian; original press, personnel and finance ledgers not examined; no allegation stated as proven.
